record.question:
A service provider exposes an EC2 logging service through an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer. The NLB was created with a security group and enforces its inbound rules for PrivateLink traffic. Consumer endpoint connections are accepted, and consumer-side networking is verified. Provider-side flow logs show rejected traffic between the NLB and its targets, and some NLB listener traffic is blocked.

Which changes address the provider-side network controls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Update the NACLs on the NLB and target subnets to allow the relevant application and health-check traffic between those subnets, including response traffic on ephemeral ports.
Update the provider target-subnet NACLs to permit only the consumer interface-endpoint subnet CIDRs as sources of application and health-check traffic.
Allow client private-IP ranges on the NLB listener port. Permit NLB outbound target and health-check traffic, and reference the NLB security group in the target security group.
Allow only the consumer client-IP ranges in the target security group. Use those same ranges as the sources for the NLB health-check port.
Update the Auto Scaling launch template to use the latest AMI and larger EC2 instances so that the NLB bypasses the rejected flows.

explanation.text:
Select <<1>> and <<3>>. NACLs are stateless, so the provider subnet rules must permit both the forward traffic and the return path. Target security groups can reference the NLB security group for the target and health-check ports. The NLB must also be able to send those requests through its outbound rules.

When NLB inbound-rule enforcement is enabled for PrivateLink, the source evaluated at that boundary is the client's private IP address, not the endpoint ENI address. <<2>> therefore uses the wrong peer for the provider NLB-to-target path. <<4>> applies the consumer source ranges at the wrong target boundary and fails to authorize NLB health checks. <<5>> changes compute capacity, which cannot override a network deny.

Treat the consumer endpoint, NLB listener and NLB-to-target connection as distinct enforcement points. Some designs deliberately disable NLB inbound-rule enforcement for PrivateLink, but this question keeps it enabled. The NLB was explicitly created with a security group because one cannot be added later to an NLB created without any.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [NLB security groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-security-groups.html). [NLB target networking](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/target-group-register-targets.html).

diagram_alt: PrivateLink listener filtering uses client private IPs, while backend security groups reference the NLB and NACLs permit both directions.

sources.supports: Targets can reference the NLB security group; enforced inbound PrivateLink rules evaluate the client private IP.
Target and load-balancer subnet NACLs must permit application, health-check and return traffic.

editorial_notes: Added evidence that faults are provider-side and specified NLB security-group creation and enforcement settings.
Retained answer set 1 and 3 and removed any suggestion that endpoint CIDRs are the enforced NLB inbound source.
